newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan defence paper urges watch on China.
newsitem.headline: Japan defence paper urges watch on China.

text.p: Japan on Tuesday called on China to be more transparent about its military strength and spending and cautioned that Beijing's military modernisation programme needed close watching.

Japan's defence ministry, in its annual Defence White Paper, also said a "revolution" was under way in weapons technology in general and said it needed new defence-related laws to go with its upgraded military ties with the United States.

"The pace of China's military modernisation is expected to be gradual," the report said. "But we must continue to pay attention to the modernisation of its air force, navy and nuclear arms, the expansion of its maritime activity and the situation on the Taiwan Strait..."
Japan said in last year's report for the first time that it must "watch" China's growing military profile after downgrading the threat from Russia, its traditional foe.
Tuesday's report said: "Although inflation must be taken into consideration, it may be said that the figure of defence spending made public by China is only a fraction of the actual amount."
China did not include development and research funds in reports of its military outlays and concealed where it re-invested cash from foreign sales of weapons in its defence industry.
Despite concern about China's future military plans, the report said North Korea remained Japan's biggest security headache because Pyongyang was a "serious source of instability" in the region.
"We must continue to keep a high degree of caution because North Korea maintains a very closed system and its moves are by no means clear," the report said.

It repeated Japan's "grave concern" over North Korea's missile programme and urged Pyongyang to adhere to a 1995 agreement with the United States to dismantle its nuclear reactors, suspected of producing weapons-grade plutonium.
For the first time, the report highlighted the importance of advanced military technology, such as pinpoint bombing by U.S. forces during the 1991 Gulf War.
"In the past, securing an edge in technology was important because it often decided the outcome of battles. Now, civilian technology has made rapid advances such as in computers.

"It may be said that the transfer of this kind of technology to the military field represents a 'revolutionary' development comparable with the emergence of aircraft or nuclear weapons," the report said.

It recommended that Japan should enact new laws to prepare for regional contingencies as part of Tokyo taking up an expanded security role. The new role has arisen from a major post-Cold War review of the U.S.-Japan military alliance.

"The Defence Agency (ministry) maintains that it is desirable that these emergency laws should be enacted, but these laws require a high degree of political decision and we must pay attention to parliament and public opinion."

However, the report said an expanded military role should be within the bounds of Japan's 1947 pacifist constitution, which bans the country from settling international disputes with the threat or use of military force.
Last week, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto's ruling party said it will submit a set of new military contingency laws to for approval by parliament next year.

They include provisions for Japan's military, or the Self-Defence Forces, to take part in naval blockades sanctioned by the United Nations and to deal with armed refugees and spies trying to enter the country.
